collection.title: The Weight of Wonders
collection.subtitle: Follow a river through a storm-bird’s orchard, an inhabited dam and a sanctuary that keeps the names of its refugees. Each place survives by passing a cost downstream.
collection.opening:
The city missed a breath at dawn.

Mara noticed because the tea did not tremble. For twenty-three years the cup had rattled against its saucer every seventeenth count, when the upper chambers let their pressure into the mountain. That morning the surface lay flat.

Below the window, ferrymen were already taking their ropes off the public hooks. Nobody rang the alarm. Bells were for accidents. This was something older.

Her father set down the bread knife.

“Take your coat,” he said.

She looked at the dry ceiling, the ordinary bread, the cup that would not move.

“Which one?”

“The one you can swim in.”

On the stair, their neighbor was tying a bedsheet through the handles of a trunk. Her husband had died on the lower ferry in winter. She had spent the spring learning to sleep without hearing his key in the door.

“Leave it,” Mara’s father said.

“It has his things.”

He knelt and tested the knot instead.

Mara went ahead with the pressure key knocking against her thigh. At the seventeenth step she stopped. A sound had come through the stone: a bearing taking weight, slowly, as if the mountain were settling into a chair. Below it lay the clean click of the lower locks closing.

The inspection board beside the landing still showed green. Someone had painted over the lowest district on its little map. Not recently. The paint had cracked.

She put her thumb against the crack and lifted one flake away. Under it, in the same neat hand as the maintenance instructions, were three words.

Permitted to flood.

Behind her, the trunk scraped the stair. Her father had taken one end. The neighbor carried the other. Neither had a hand free for the rail.

Mara turned the pressure key in the inspection door. It would cost her the apprenticeship. That seemed, suddenly, a very small thing to lose.

trilogy.title: The City That Holds Its Breath
trilogy.premise: An apprentice pressure keeper exposes the decision that made the poorest district expendable. Saving the city breaks trust in its custodians.

trilogy.title: The Names We Carried
trilogy.premise: Displaced families discover that sanctuary has altered their legal lives. A witness must decide which truths can be restored without exposing the people they protect.

trilogy.title: The Orchard Above the Storm
trilogy.premise: The rebuilt dam cannot distribute water fairly while upstream collectors monopolize rain. Workers and custodians negotiate who will carry the cost of repair.

entries.name: Orvess
entries.title: The Last Abutment
entries.summary: An ancient flood engine still protects a boundary that leaves half its city outside. Saving it means changing what it was built to save.
history: Orvess was commissioned to prevent a particular flood, not to govern a city. Settlements accumulated in its maintenance galleries over generations. Its original operating boundary never changed. When a contaminated pressure signal predicts the ancient disaster again, the machine prepares to seal the lower districts as sacrificial overflow chambers.
It is not angry. It is working from a definition of safety that no longer includes everyone.
storySeeds: An engineer’s parent signed the obsolete evacuation boundary. Write the moment the engineer finds the signature while people wait for a safe route.
The replacement bearing belongs to another working settlement. Give its envoy a defensible reason to refuse the loan.

image.alt: Orvess braces bronze and ceramic limbs across a flooded dam, a working water conduit through its torso and a tiny engineer on the foreground gantry.

sessionKit.prompt: Write or run a scene in Arcanea’s experimental Weight of Wonders setting, centered on Orvess. An engineer’s parent signed the obsolete evacuation boundary. Write the moment the engineer finds the signature while people wait for a safe route. Keep the danger observable, give each affected person a concrete stake, and carry one consequence into the next scene. Treat these concepts as proposals; do not change locked Arcanea identities.
beats: Show the failed pressure rhythm through an ordinary object.
Teach one audible sweep tell before forcing a crossing.
Put a named household and valuable stores on competing routes.
Ask who will maintain the repaired machine after the heroes leave.

entries.entrance: The party hears a lockkeeper complain that the city has missed a breath. Ferry ropes tighten. Every workshop lamp leans in the same draft. Outside, a hillside rises; what looked like a mineral face is a shoulder. Orvess reaches past the party to catch a failing gate.

encounter.objective: Restore a safe pressure sequence while keeping an evacuation route open. Combat buys access and time; damage alone does not solve the crisis.

phases.title: The old instruction
phases.description: When the lower basin reaches its first marker, Orvess sweeps intruders from the control gantries. Shoulder bearings lock audibly before each sweep. Players cross during weight transfer and use raised service recesses as cover.

phases.title: The price of pressure
phases.description: Opening an emergency bypass exposes the damaged hip regulator. Pressure jets now cross the arena at intervals announced by rising sediment and vibrating pipes. Players redirect jets into abandoned channels; striking the exposed regulator indiscriminately worsens the flood.

phases.title: A different boundary
phases.description: Once two evacuation routes are secured, the party must hold a replacement signal in place while Orvess braces a final surge. A temporary vulnerability allows a fast kill, but preserving the engine requires surviving its last automatic defensive cycle.

endings.label: Repair the protector
endings.consequence: Controlled flooding destroys valuable stores while evacuation routes preserve more homes. The city inherits a maintenance obligation and a public argument over compensation.

endings.label: Destroy Orvess
endings.consequence: The defensive cycle stops immediately. Without the engine holding the surge, the lower city floods; the next story begins with displacement and responsibility.

endings.label: Evacuate and withdraw
endings.consequence: Warn the lower districts and move whoever the surviving routes can carry. Orvess remains unstable, homes are abandoned, and returning requires a second operation.

entries.artNote: The image establishes the colossus’s weight and working conduit. Exact scale, movement and hydraulic behavior remain design proposals.
bodyMovement: Its bronze bearings polish where they move; ceramic plates retain mineral deposits from former flood levels. The chest opening is a working water conduit, not an ornamental weak spot. A narrow amber leak at the hip marks pressure loss. Its limbs move in deliberate sequences: plant, transfer load, test resistance, commit. A giant should not turn like a human wearing a large costume.

entries.name: The City That Holds Its Breath
entries.title: An inhabited pressure vault
entries.summary: Families have made homes inside a dam’s maintenance galleries. Every new route changes the water beneath somebody’s floor.
history: Three routes remain understandable from the first major vista: an upper spiral inspection stair, a middle market bridge, and a lower ferry basin. They reconnect through valve rooms, abandoned spillways and family-built passages. Opening a shortcut can change the water level somewhere already visited.
storySeeds: A ferryman knows an unmarked passage but will not leave the people who cannot pay. Let the rising water force a decision before anyone finishes arguing.
A salvage diver brings up two objects: proof of an old sacrifice and the part needed to stop a new one. Only one can survive the crossing.

image.alt: A spiral inspection stair, inhabited market bridge and ferry basin descend through a huge pressure vault beside a suspended counterweight.

sessionKit.prompt: Write or run a scene in Arcanea’s experimental Weight of Wonders setting, centered on The City That Holds Its Breath. A ferryman knows an unmarked passage but will not leave the people who cannot pay. Let the rising water force a decision before anyone finishes arguing. Keep the danger observable, give each affected person a concrete stake, and carry one consequence into the next scene. Treat these concepts as proposals; do not change locked Arcanea identities.
beats: Start at a market stall that must pack while trading.
Let the party see all three routes from one overlook.
Reveal the old flood mark beside an inhabited doorway.
Change a previously safe route after a valve is opened.

place.spatialIdentity: An inhabited vertical pressure vault. The upper inspection stair, middle market bridge and lower ferry basin remain visible together, then reconnect through working valve rooms.
ecology: Lockkeepers listen for pressure changes; silt divers recover tools from warm bearing pools.
Canal shrimp feed around mineral deposits while families hang evacuation ropes beside their laundry.
routes: Upper stair: a dry inspection route exposed to the engine’s maintenance sweep.
Market bridge: workshops and family passages connect to valve rooms.
Lower basin: ferry travel opens when the salvage level floods.
discoveries: Flood marks contradict the official account of an earlier sealing.
Repair records trace diverted bronze to military supply.
A memorial stands above homes that were occupied during the last sacrifice.
place.consequence: Flooding the salvage level opens a ferry shortcut and destroys recoverable evidence. Draining it preserves records but exposes the party to maintenance sweeps.

entries.artNote: The banners are incidental details in the artwork, not approved faction emblems. Routes described here would need spatial testing in a playable adaptation.

entries.name: Vesrane
entries.title: Keeper of Borrowed Faces
entries.summary: She lent the dead’s identities to people who needed to disappear. Now she decides who is allowed to become themselves again.
history: Vesrane began lending the names of the dead to people fleeing targeted persecution. A borrowed identity could conceal a family from a hostile registry. The process required an original name to be held in escrow, so one person could not claim several lives.

The emergency ended unevenly. The institution endured. Returning a name now risks exposing the people sheltered behind it; withholding it leaves a survivor unable to prove a marriage, inheritance or promise. Vesrane knows the harms in exact detail. She continues because she distrusts anyone who promises an easy alternative.
storySeeds: A borrowed name has inherited a debt and a marriage. Write a meeting where three people can each tell the truth and still contradict one another.
Vesrane recognizes a witness she once saved. Let her make a precise offer that would protect that person and harm someone absent.

image.alt: Vesrane, a mature woman in a black coat with one pale fold, holds a porcelain mask and a taut dark thread in a flooded limestone registry.

sessionKit.prompt: Write or run a scene in Arcanea’s experimental Weight of Wonders setting, centered on Vesrane. A borrowed name has inherited a debt and a marriage. Write a meeting where three people can each tell the truth and still contradict one another. Keep the danger observable, give each affected person a concrete stake, and carry one consequence into the next scene. Treat these concepts as proposals; do not change locked Arcanea identities.
beats: Offer a useful identity before revealing its cost.
Demonstrate recognition with a harmless door.
Have a consenting witness refuse one part of the plan.
Let the selected ending change who can safely testify.

entries.entrance: A refugee calls the player by a name they have never used. Vesrane corrects the refugee gently, then offers the player a mask. The person who accepts it finds that the palace's doors recognize them.

encounter.objective: Recover a particular identity without exposing the refugees who borrowed from it.

phases.title: Recognition
phases.description: Accepting a borrowed name changes which doors and sentries admit the player. A mask tilts before Vesrane redirects a route. Players must track their current identity through physical tokens and environmental response, not invisible guessing.

phases.title: The witness
phases.description: Taking the original record awakens reflections that repeat previously performed attacks. Wet floor ripples announce repetition; dry ledges break the reflection cycle. Changing tactics matters more than increasing damage.

phases.title: The return
phases.description: The party can sever the keeper's central thread, disabling the palace and exposing every protected identity, or distribute the testimony among consenting witnesses and defeat her attempt to prevent the transfer.

endings.label: Return names through witnesses
endings.consequence: Consenting witnesses distribute the testimony. Some people regain their names; others choose continued concealment. Vesrane survives as an adversarial witness, and disputed claims still require a hearing.

endings.label: Sever the central thread
endings.consequence: The palace loses control of recognition. Every protected identity becomes exposed, including people who did not consent; the party must face the pursuit and contested claims that follow.

endings.label: Negotiate one protected return
endings.consequence: Secure the requested name with its bearer’s consent while preserving other refugees’ cover. The wider coercive system remains, and the party must explain whose freedom it postponed.

entries.artNote: The portrait establishes Vesrane’s face, coat, mask and thread. The proposed face-omitting reflection is a story direction, not a clearly visible event in this image.
bodyMovement: She has a mature, particular face, ordinary human proportions and controlled movement. Her power appears through a small action: a thread drawn taut, a reflection losing correspondence, a mask turning toward a voice. Her expression carries more threat than a cloud of effects.

entries.name: The Palace of Unreturned Names
entries.title: A sanctuary with a price
entries.summary: A flooded registry recognizes the name you carry. Its oldest exit was closed by an order, not a curse.
history: Tall limestone stelae divide a flooded registry into narrow passages. Alcoves hold sparse porcelain masks; empty niches matter as much as occupied ones. A side gallery overlooks routes that become visible in reflection before they appear above the water.

The palace should never become arbitrary dream logic. A borrowed identity consistently admits the bearer to its associated district. Water reveals the next eligible route. Dry stone preserves a stable path back. Players learn these rules through safe examples before any encounter demands them.
storySeeds: An empty mask niche receives fresh flowers every week. Discover who tends it without making the answer a hidden monster.
Two refugees carry papers for the same identity. Build the scene around what each fears losing, before anyone asks which document is authentic.

image.alt: Sparse porcelain masks occupy tall limestone stelae above black water; a refugee procession follows stepping stones past a registration counter.

sessionKit.prompt: Write or run a scene in Arcanea’s experimental Weight of Wonders setting, centered on The Palace of Unreturned Names. An empty mask niche receives fresh flowers every week. Discover who tends it without making the answer a hidden monster. Keep the danger observable, give each affected person a concrete stake, and carry one consequence into the next scene. Treat these concepts as proposals; do not change locked Arcanea identities.
beats: Introduce a registrar doing necessary, ordinary work.
Demonstrate the same name opening the same district twice.
Show the older exit beneath later masonry.
Return by dry stone so the impossible rule stays legible.

place.spatialIdentity: Narrow limestone registry aisles cross shallow black water. A borrowed identity consistently admits its bearer to one district; reflections reveal the next eligible route, while dry stone provides a stable return.
ecology: Registrars, refugees and voluntary witnesses continue their work inside the disputed institution.
Administrative traces repeat limited actions; encountering one does not automatically begin a fight.
routes: A safe entrance teaches recognition with a door before any pursuit.
A side gallery overlooks the next route in reflection.
The dry stone return path stays accessible as identities change.
discoveries: An ordinary child’s shoe survives a hurried departure.
A dry room holds freely offered identities never requested back.
New masonry blocks an older exit: confinement came from a policy change.
place.consequence: Restoring recognition changes whose testimony can travel safely. Treat consent and the possibility of renewed persecution as consequences of the route chosen.

entries.artNote: The distant route can read as a reflection or submerged stone. A playable adaptation would need a tested visual cue; the rules below describe the intended encounter.

entries.name: Qorath
entries.title: The Storm’s Heir
entries.summary: A vast territorial bird attacks the collectors that threaten its nest. Those same towers keep the richest orchards watered.
history: Qorath's species nests where ridge thermals intersect moisture-bearing winds. Its flight does not create weather from nothing. It concentrates and redirects local updrafts, a bounded fantasy adaptation with visible effects on cloud, petals, cloth and water.

Farmers have learned to cultivate beneath those flight paths. New collector towers now force more moisture toward profitable terraces and dry neighboring land. Qorath attacks the towers because their pressure changes threaten its nesting cleft. From below, the attacks look like an animal turning against its beneficiaries.
storySeeds: An orchard keeper can predict Qorath’s next pass but refuses to abandon the harvest that pays the village’s winter debt.
A wounded scavenger reaches a terrace before Qorath does. Let the smallest animal reveal what the collectors have changed.

image.alt: A colossal rust-breasted bird with slate-blue face banks over an orchard keeper, its long pale wings opening above immense storm clouds.

sessionKit.prompt: Write or run a scene in Arcanea’s experimental Weight of Wonders setting, centered on Qorath. An orchard keeper can predict Qorath’s next pass but refuses to abandon the harvest that pays the village’s winter debt. Keep the danger observable, give each affected person a concrete stake, and carry one consequence into the next scene. Treat these concepts as proposals; do not change locked Arcanea identities.
beats: Let petals move before the bird appears.
Teach a sheltered crossing before the exposed aqueduct.
Give a worker a reason to protect a collector.
Account for both nesting territory and the next harvest.

entries.entrance: Blossom stops falling and travels sideways. A shadow crosses several terraces at once. Qorath passes close enough for the player to hear separate feathers flex.

encounter.objective: Reconfigure three collectors without destroying the nest or depriving the inhabited terraces of water.

phases.title: Warning pass
phases.description: Crossing a marked nesting boundary triggers low territorial flights. Loose petals announce the wake before it arrives. Players use rooted stone windbreaks and move after the trailing wing passes.

phases.title: The stolen current
phases.description: Disabling the first collector changes thermal flow. Qorath circles to regain lift, opening windows for crossing aqueduct spans. Breaking arbitrary supports can strand the bird over inhabited terraces.

phases.title: A place to land
phases.description: With the collectors balanced, players clear a safe landing approach while protecting workers from residual gusts. The encounter ends through restored territory, forced retreat or a lethal choice with ecological consequences.

endings.label: Restore the nesting boundary
endings.consequence: Balanced collectors give Qorath a safe approach and restore some neighboring water. The richest terraces lose part of their yield; workers need a say in how that loss is shared.

endings.label: Force Qorath to retreat
endings.consequence: A temporary opening lets workers finish the crossing. The altered currents and threatened nest remain, so the danger returns unless the collectors change.

endings.label: Kill Qorath
endings.consequence: The immediate route becomes safer, but water distribution and scavenger ecology deteriorate. The next season tests whether the settlement can replace the functions it destroyed.

entries.artNote: The near wing extends beyond the frame. The image does not establish an exact wingspan; full proportions and flight behavior remain to be developed.
bodyMovement: The design has two wings and two legs. Feather wear, muscle mass, wing loading and turns must remain consistent in future depictions. The proposed enormous span is a design target; the cinematic's perspective does not validate a precise measurement or a flight simulation.

entries.name: The Orchard Above the Storm
entries.title: A cultivated wilderness
entries.summary: Fruit trees grow above the thunderclouds. Across the ridge, a carefully maintained channel has been dry for three years.
history: The first view begins inside a garden. Fruit, pruning, irrigation and hands establish ordinary scale before the vista opens into ridges, bridges and thundercloud. Every inhabited platform attaches to bedrock. This avoids using floating islands as an automatic substitute for wonder.
storySeeds: A worker maintains a channel that carries no water because stopping would surrender the village’s claim. Write the day an upstream visitor offers to buy it.
The richest terrace agrees to surrender water, then discovers that its hired pickers will bear the first loss. Let the workers revise the bargain.

image.alt: An orchard worker repairs a windbreak among fruit terraces, water channels and houses rooted in sunlit cliffs above a vast storm.

sessionKit.prompt: Write or run a scene in Arcanea’s experimental Weight of Wonders setting, centered on The Orchard Above the Storm. A worker maintains a channel that carries no water because stopping would surrender the village’s claim. Write the day an upstream visitor offers to buy it. Keep the danger observable, give each affected person a concrete stake, and carry one consequence into the next scene. Treat these concepts as proposals; do not change locked Arcanea identities.
beats: Begin with pruning or irrigation at human scale.
Reveal the storm only after the work feels familiar.
Follow a dry but maintained channel upstream.
Invite the people losing water to alter the proposed settlement.

place.spatialIdentity: Working gardens lead to narrow aqueducts above thundercloud. Every terrace attaches to bedrock; exposed crossings and protected collector interiors offer different risks.
ecology: Gardeners and ridge porters share the terraces with pollinators and seed-eating cliff mammals.
Scavengers follow Qorath’s feeding grounds; changing its territory changes their access to food.
routes: Sheltered orchard path: learn the wind from petals and cloth.
Ridge aqueduct: the fastest crossing has the greatest exposure.
Collector interiors: protected vertical shortcuts change external flow when operated.
discoveries: Older terraces share water; recent collectors intercept it.
A dry channel bears regular tool marks, proving that neglect did not cause the shortage.
A thick broken eggshell establishes the nesting scale without exposing a hatchling.
place.consequence: Rebalancing water helps deprived terraces but costs the richest gardens yield. Ask who owns the crop and who is paid only when it is harvested.

entries.artNote: The image shows a working, cultivated landscape. The dry-channel discovery and unequal water allocation belong to the story proposal, rather than facts proved by the painting.

entries.name: Tharvoss
entries.title: The Undertow Maw
entries.summary: A river predator has learned that a boat bell means trapped prey. Reopen the migration stair, survive its suction strike and take the crossing back.
history: Tharvoss once followed the seasonal silver-run between the estuary and the mountain basins. Its digging kept deep-water refuges open through dry months. A toll order closed the fish passages while leaving the main spillways flowing. The migrating fish accumulated below the gates; the predator followed them into a place too narrow for a large animal to retreat safely.

The keepers now face an individual that attacks supply boats deliberately. A displaced animal can still be a lethal enemy. The objective is to stop those attacks and reopen the crossing, whether the party drives Tharvoss into a safe downstream channel or kills it. Removing the animal alone leaves the broken passage ready to produce the next crisis.

Local families call the old sluice bell the drowned father's supper call. That belief became practical knowledge: Tharvoss associated its sound with fish released from sorting pens. The tale is an inhabitant belief, not a new Arcanean deity. Othrek's tariff seal on the closure order links this encounter to the Brine Tribunal.
storySeeds: A boat builder recognizes the bell on a wreck as one she sold to the keepers. Give her useful knowledge and a reason she has avoided the inquiry.
Write the first safe crossing after victory from the view of a child carrying a basket too large for their hands; show which adult still refuses to board.

image.alt: A vast low river predator draws water into its pleated throat beside an adult keeper on a raised stair; closed sluices and stranded boats frame its mineral-armored back.

entries.artNote: The artwork establishes mass, a suction-oriented throat and raised refuges. The far-side limbs are occluded; exact eighteen-metre scale, pressure physics and the banner designs remain unapproved design details.

growth.practice: Read the water before reading the monster: inward-moving foam and throat expansion announce suction. Reach the buttress recess rather than rolling blindly into the flooded lane.
growth.mastery: Reopen both fish passages while keeping the supply gantry intact and never using a living person as bait. Success requires positioning, patience and coordination.
growth.reward: The crossing reopens. Keepers teach the proposed Anchor Step technique, which lets a prepared fighter brace at marked solid cover against a sustained pull; it is a situational skill, not general knockback immunity.
growth.rematch: At high water one refuge is submerged and a second safe position must be created by lowering a service platform. The same cues remain readable; increased difficulty changes decisions rather than hiding information.

sessionKit.prompt: Write or run a scene around Tharvoss. Begin with a visible ecological clue, teach one safe response before escalating danger, and make victory change a named person's next day. Preserve the selected outcome and distinguish these EXPERIMENTAL proposals from locked Arcanea canon.
beats: Show foam moving against the ordinary current before the first strike.
Let the party test a buttress recess during a harmless gate release.
Use the bell to move Tharvoss while a keeper opens the passage.
Show the first supply boat crossing and name who repairs the damaged gantry.

entries.entrance: A sorting bell rings twice. The fish stop breaking the surface. An empty skiff slides sideways against the current; then the lower pool lifts around a broad mineral-plated back. Tharvoss ignores the nearest sword and turns toward the occupied supply boat.
bodyMovement: Four short weight-bearing limbs support a low, wide body. A pleated throat expands before the suction strike; the tail supplies turning force in deep water. On stone it plants, pulls and pauses rather than skating. Pale mineral deposits on the dorsal plates contrast with flexible dark skin.

Its hardest attacks are short bursts. After a long pull the throat collapses, the jaw rests open and the animal must draw fresh water across its respiratory surfaces. That recovery is a combat opening. The giant anatomy is fantasy extrapolation, not a claim about a real species.
foodWeb: Role: seasonal apex predator and pool excavator; it consumes silver-run fish and large river crustaceans, while small scavengers use its abandoned feeding sites.
Dependency: connected migration channels and oxygenated refuge pools. Closed passages concentrate prey temporarily, then starve both fish and predator of viable habitat.
Disturbance: deliberate gate closure and repeated boat feeding taught this individual a dangerous association with bells and people.

After victory: reopen passage whichever resolution is chosen. If killed, recover the carcass in sections so decomposition does not consume the lower basin's oxygen; do not assume killing one animal restores the watershed.

encounter.objective: Stop attacks on occupied boats, reopen the migration passage and secure a usable crossing. Driving the animal out and killing it are both valid victories with different follow-up work.

phases.title: The water takes a breath
phases.description: Throat expansion, inward foam and two low knocks from the bell precede a sustained pull. Cross behind the planted forelimb, brace inside a buttress recess and strike the soft jaw hinge during the open-mouth recovery. Damage interrupts the next pull but does not open the gate.

phases.title: The broken feeding lane
phases.description: Opening the first passage disperses the fish. Tharvoss switches to short lateral lunges marked by a planted outer foot and a curling tail. Ring the sorting bell from an empty service platform to redirect it; a keeper can then reach the second winch. Repeating the bell without changing position lets the predator learn the lure.

phases.title: Take back the crossing
phases.description: With the downstream chute open, a correctly timed gate release creates an escape current. Hold the gantry while Tharvoss commits to it, or use the final exhausted recovery to kill the boat-hunting individual. Both routes end the immediate threat; the party must keep civilians off the surge lane.

endings.label: Drive Tharvoss downstream
endings.consequence: The crossing reopens and the predator enters an uninhabited refuge channel. Keepers stop baiting the bell and monitor the channel; this is managed separation, not domestication.

endings.label: Kill the boat hunter
endings.consequence: The immediate predator is defeated. Salvage crews gain durable dorsal plates, but must remove the carcass and repair the migration gate before the basin can recover.

endings.label: Sacrifice the toll gate
endings.consequence: Destroy the gate supports to restore flow quickly and force the beast into the lower reach. Boats return sooner, but workers lose a useful flood-control structure and must build a safer replacement.

entries.name: The Spawning Stair
entries.title: The river remembers a way through
entries.summary: Seven inhabited river basins turn a migration into a gauntlet. Find the closed passage, learn the keeper's routes and give the river back its way through.
history: The stair began as a series of natural travertine shelves. Keepers added narrow fish passages, service ledges and adjustable gates rather than replacing the whole river with one wall. Houses grew beside the work. The place is both habitat and public infrastructure.

A new toll administration closed the side passages to concentrate fish in licensed sorting pools. The main falls still ran, so visitors assumed the river was healthy. Boat attacks revealed the cost long after the first spawning season failed. The missing maintenance boards were sold to repair the Tribunal's private cisterns.
storySeeds: Write a dispute between a keeper who wants to save the working gate and a fisher who can no longer wait for a careful repair.
Let a party discover that a feared empty house still receives a daily meal: its owner is hiding workers who refused the closure order.

image.alt: Adult keepers haul a gate board up a continuous cliff stair beside terraced falls, a crowded fish passage and a broad predator wake in the lower basin.

entries.artNote: The scene conveys migration pressure and three route types. Fish passage heights, structural loads and continuous navigation need a separate playable layout; the painted falls are not an engineering specification.

growth.practice: Trace water and movement separately. A visible waterfall does not prove that fish, boats or people can pass it safely.
growth.mastery: Restore a continuous migration route, move the last supply boat and preserve one dry civilian exit through the changing water levels.
growth.reward: The keepers reopen a route between settlements and provide a portable current marker that reveals surface-flow changes when deployed. It supports observation rather than solving navigation automatically.
growth.rematch: A storm raises the lower basin before the repair is finished. Reuse the learned route logic with one bridge lost and a family waiting on the wrong bank.

sessionKit.prompt: Write or run a scene around The Spawning Stair. Begin with a visible ecological clue, teach one safe response before escalating danger, and make victory change a named person's next day. Preserve the selected outcome and distinguish these EXPERIMENTAL proposals from locked Arcanea canon.
beats: Begin with a full lower pool and an empty upstream sorting net.
Teach the dry stair, gantry and service channel as distinct routes.
Find the tariff order and the missing-board receipt in separate locations.
Finish with migrating fish passing a repaired channel while supplies cross overhead.

place.spatialIdentity: Seven broad stepped basins, a cliff-side maintenance stair, inhabited crossing gantries and a low service channel. The useful fish passages run beside the main falls; closed gates break the route even while water continues downstream.
ecology: Silver-run fish carry nutrients between the estuary and mountain reaches; their eggs and young require places that adults can actually reach.
Tharvoss follows the migration. Its deep excavated pools shelter smaller animals during dry months, but a trapped hunting individual threatens the inhabited crossings.
Reeds slow sediment at basin margins. Removing every reed bed improves sightlines temporarily while worsening erosion and eliminating small-fish cover.
Gate repairs change water level, oxygenation and passage together. These effects provide encounter choices; their exact values require playtesting.
routes: Cliff stair: slow, dry and defensible; haul the missing board here before the water rises.
Sorting gantry: fastest access to the central winch, exposed to suction and a lateral tail strike.
Service channel: a concealed low route to the second gate, usable only after reading the current marker and lowering the side flow.
discoveries: An obsolete public migration schedule contradicts the new tariff order.
Tool wear shows the side passage was locked deliberately rather than jammed by silt.
A boat bell with a repaired crack explains why the predator turns toward certain supply runs.
place.consequence: A restored passage changes the next season as well as the next crossing. The closure order and repair receipts can become evidence against Othrek; destroying them may win the fight while losing the public case.

entries.name: The Glassroot Hunger
entries.title: A colony that learned the taste of living roots
entries.summary: A luminous colonial animal has outgrown a seed vault. Break its feeding network, protect the nursery and defeat a threat that has no single head to cut off.
history: Small colonies once consumed dead roots in the archive's drainage pools. Salt intrusion killed a whole root terrace and produced a sudden nutrient pulse. The surviving colony grew into the abandoned space, then extended its feeding ribbons into living roots and stored nursery feed.

The keepers call it the tree's second soul. That poetic explanation delayed action: cutting a feeding stem was treated as an attack on the forest itself. The archive record instead shows a colony with specialized feeding, defensive and fluid-storage structures. It can be studied, contained and fought.

Othrek's opened saline bypass accelerated the root damage. His responsibility does not remove the immediate danger: the Hunger has begun pulling sluice covers aside to reach new food. Stopping the colony and stopping the contaminated inflow are separate objectives.
storySeeds: A keeper who defended the second-soul story must guide the first cutting team. Let them retain dignity by noticing something the skeptics missed.
Write the moment a fighter stops searching for a face and begins seeing the sequence of feeding bells.

image.alt: A huge translucent, question-mark-shaped colony rises from a flooded seed vault; specialized bells line a carbonate stem and amber ribbons lift a heavy sluice cover.

entries.artNote: The image establishes a distinctive colonial body plan, translucency and a lifted cover. Its freshwater, rooted, giant biology is fantasy extrapolation from marine colonial organisms; anatomical function and twenty-metre scale remain proposals. The upper organ is treated as a supported reservoir; it must not be modeled as providing buoyancy while above water.

growth.practice: Read a sequence across several body parts. A feeding bell contracts before its paired ribbon pulls; a defensive cup opens before it releases the slowing mucous sheet.
growth.mastery: Interrupt the three supply stems in the correct order while preserving the clean nursery pool and rescuing the keeper on the lower ledge.
growth.reward: The seed vault survives. Keepers teach a proposed Pulse Reading technique: after observing a repeating mechanism or organism, the character can mark its next opening for allies. It rewards observation and does not reveal unseen enemies.
growth.rematch: Two feeding stems alternate their timing while the lower path floods. The cue sequence remains consistent; the party must divide attention and assign roles instead of relying on higher damage.

sessionKit.prompt: Write or run a scene around The Glassroot Hunger. Begin with a visible ecological clue, teach one safe response before escalating danger, and make victory change a named person's next day. Preserve the selected outcome and distinguish these EXPERIMENTAL proposals from locked Arcanea canon.
beats: Show a harmless small colony completing one feeding cycle.
Let the party identify a supply stem by following the amber flow.
Force a choice between a fast cut and protecting the clean nursery pool.
End with a saved seed case being carried back into daylight.

entries.entrance: The archive's drainage bells have gone silent. A heavy stone cover rises without a hand beneath it, suspended by an amber ribbon. In the pool beyond, translucent bells contract one after another along a curved ivory stem. Only then does the entire colony lift into the sun shaft.
bodyMovement: A curved, weight-bearing carbonate keel anchors in submerged roots and supports a translucent fluid reservoir. Repeating bells, feeding ribbons and protective cups have different jobs and visible connections to the same stem. The silhouette has a large central opening; it is not a humanoid hidden inside tentacles.

The colony moves by coordinated contraction, bracing against submerged roots before pulling. The reservoir changes volume slowly; narrow feeding ribbons move quickly. A damaged bell changes the timing of the next section rather than making the whole organism spin or teleport.
foodWeb: Role: normally a small colonial consumer of decaying root material and microorganisms in the drainage pools. The boss is an exceptional overgrown colony, not every colony of its kind.
Dependency: water exchange, dissolved nutrients and the archive's root network. Its giant fantasy form also depends on light reaching symbiotic tissue in the upper chamber.
Disturbance: salt intrusion killed a root terrace, then persistent nutrient access favored a colony that began consuming living tissue.
After victory: close the contaminated inflow and restore the clean nursery channel. Destroying the giant colony without repairing the water system leaves the conditions for another bloom.

encounter.objective: Disable the giant colony's feeding network, preserve a viable seed nursery and close the contaminated supply. The fight rewards recognizing specialized parts and coordinating interruptions.

phases.title: Learn the feeding rhythm
phases.description: Bells contract from the upper stem downward before their ribbons sweep the lower path. Cross during the pause at the final bell, cut the exposed supply sheath and retreat to a dry root buttress. A small harmless colony near the entrance teaches the same sequence first.

phases.title: The divided body
phases.description: After the first supply stem is cut, defensive cups open and spread slow-moving mucous sheets across the pool. Break a cup while it opens to create a clean crossing; severing every nearby stem at once releases concentrated feed into the nursery and makes the next wave stronger.

phases.title: Keep something alive
phases.description: The upper reservoir tips toward the clean pool as the root anchors lose their hold. One ally operates the diversion sluice while the others interrupt two alternating ribbon pulls. Expose and cut the final coordinating stem before the colony anchors in the nursery. The defeated body collapses into the isolated drainage basin.

endings.label: Isolate and destroy the giant colony
endings.consequence: The nursery remains viable and the immediate threat ends. Keepers remove the dead mass in stages, retain harmless study colonies and repair the salt breach.

endings.label: Evacuate the seeds and purge the vault
endings.consequence: The colony is defeated with a broad cleansing flood after the seed cases are carried out. The archive loses fragile root habitats and needs seasons of restoration, but its people and seed stock survive.

endings.label: Sever its supply and contain it
endings.consequence: The party isolates the giant in an empty drainage chamber and ends its access to living roots. Containment needs a funded watch and a kill plan if the chamber fails; it is not a promise that the predator becomes friendly.

entries.name: The Glassroot Sepulchre
entries.title: A nursery beneath the old forest
entries.summary: An immense root-vault stores the forest's future. Follow the line between living moss and salt-killed roots before the Hunger reaches the clean nursery.
history: The seed keepers built dry ceramic vaults between the buttress roots of an ancient tree. Wet lower channels carried drainage away; high shelves kept seed cases above ordinary floods. The archive grew through maintenance and grafting, not through a forgotten civilization's impossible technology.

A recent saline bypass has contaminated one side of the root system. The dead terrace fed an explosive colonial bloom. The oldest keepers noticed the changing taste of the water before any monster appeared, but the Tribunal dismissed their samples as a storage dispute. Their dated jars can now prove the sequence.
storySeeds: A keeper must choose which seed cases fit in one boat. Give every proposed selection a future community that depends on it.
Write a quiet scene in the healthy alcove after the battle, where the return of one small bird means more than a speech.

image.alt: A keeper samples the channel beneath monumental forest roots; green living moss and a small bird occupy one bank while salt crust and amber colonial growth cover the other.

entries.artNote: The painting makes healthy and damaged root zones visible. Water color and cloth alone do not prove salinity; the story requires retained samples and archive records. Continuous traversal and root-load behavior need level design.

growth.practice: Separate symptoms from causes. Trace the white deposits upstream and compare dated samples before blaming every organism in the pool.
growth.mastery: Carry viable seed cases through a route that remains dry, close the salt breach and preserve the living root bridge.
growth.reward: The rescued nursery can supply a restoration garden in a later community chapter. Keepers share a field kit for collecting and comparing water samples; interpretation still requires observation.
growth.rematch: The same vault during a storm has fewer dry shelves and a second evacuation party. Players apply the known water route to a harder rescue rather than repeat the identical fight.

sessionKit.prompt: Write or run a scene around The Glassroot Sepulchre. Begin with a visible ecological clue, teach one safe response before escalating danger, and make victory change a named person's next day. Preserve the selected outcome and distinguish these EXPERIMENTAL proposals from locked Arcanea canon.
beats: Begin with a bird on the healthy bank and silence on the salt-killed bank.
Compare the newest water sample with a dated archive jar.
Teach upper balcony, lower path and suspended bridge before the colony attacks.
Carry one named seed case to a place where its future planting matters.

place.spatialIdentity: A cathedral-sized root cavern with a central drainage channel, dry high seed vaults and two visually different banks: living moss on one side, recent salt damage on the other.
ecology: The tree and nursery require freshwater exchange; the archive's dry storage and wet drainage have different functions.
Small colonial consumers normally process dead material. The exceptional boss colony becomes destructive after a large root die-off and continued nutrient access.
Birds and small aquatic animals indicate habitat use, but their presence alone is not a complete water-quality test.
Restoration needs both clean inflow and removal or containment of the giant feeding mass. A spectacular kill cannot substitute for fixing the breach.
routes: Upper archive balcony: safe seed storage and the best view of feeding sequences, with a limited carrying route to the exit.
Lower caretaker path: direct access to three sluices, exposed to ribbon sweeps and rising water.
Root-to-root rope bridge: a fast evacuation route that must not be cut merely to damage the boss below.
discoveries: Dated sample jars place the salt intrusion after a Tribunal bypass order.
A healthy small colony demonstrates the boss's feeding sequence without exposing the party to lethal force.
The oldest dry alcove contains a planting map for communities displaced after the dam crisis.
place.consequence: Saving the archive gives later stories something tangible to rebuild with. Losing the records weakens the case against Othrek even if the seeds survive; losing the seeds makes a legal victory insufficient for the forest.

entries.name: Marshal Othrek
entries.title: The Salt Regent
entries.summary: A disciplined duelist controls the estuary's drinking water. Break his pressure weapon, defeat his guard and open the gate he has made people pay to survive.
history: Othrek inherited a legitimate flood-control office and converted emergency tolls into permanent rule. He closes migration passages to control fish sales, opens saline bypasses against unlicensed gardens and sells protection from shortages his own orders worsen. These are chosen acts, not possession by a hidden cosmic force.

He is a capable commander whose authority depends on a narrow fact: someone must operate the gates. He treats that expertise as proof that he should own the people downstream. Former sluice workers can expose the difference by operating the system without him.

The Salt Regent is an experimental regional antagonist. He does not replace Malachar, alter locked cosmic identities or establish a new universal force of evil. His defeat belongs to the material and political history of this proposed watershed.
storySeeds: A guard receives the order to flood the court while their family waits below. Let a prior player action determine whether they obey.
Write Othrek's first exchange with the keeper who can run the gates better than he can. Give him a sharp argument without allowing competence to excuse his cruelty.

image.alt: A weathered human marshal in practical ivory and black armor stands with a long white mantle, a squared sluice-hook polearm and a venting pressure gauntlet before a tidal fortress.

entries.artNote: The image establishes an adult human adversary, practical costume and iconic tool-shaped weapon. Exact height, pressure-system function and the implied duel motion remain design proposals; the pose is key art, not combat animation.

growth.practice: Read commitment: a planted heel precedes the long hook sweep, and a white pressure plume precedes the gauntlet burst. Parry the blade when appropriate; step outside the burst cone rather than treating every attack alike.
growth.mastery: Defeat Othrek while keeping the civilian drinking-water line open and retaining the gate orders as evidence. Skill includes timing, target priority and refusing an unnecessary environmental shortcut.
growth.reward: The water gate returns to a public keeper council. A repaired pressure bracer enables a short environmental grapple at compatible anchors; the proposed Counterweight Riposte technique rewards a correctly read committed strike. Neither grants invulnerability.
growth.rematch: A training reconstruction combines the hook sweep with alternating gate surges and a cooperating guard. Cues remain audible and visible; victory tests learned responses under overlapping pressure.

sessionKit.prompt: Write or run a scene around Marshal Othrek. Begin with a visible ecological clue, teach one safe response before escalating danger, and make victory change a named person's next day. Preserve the selected outcome and distinguish these EXPERIMENTAL proposals from locked Arcanea canon.
beats: Show a worker opening a drinking-water tap before the marshal appears.
Teach the difference between blade commitment and the pressure plume.
Put a guard's family and a public record at risk in different places.
Finish with the gate opened by ordinary keepers, making the victory visible.

entries.entrance: The drinking-water tap coughs air. Across the causeway, Othrek sets the squared edge of his polearm on the stone and lets the crowd hear it scrape. A guard closes the gate behind him. He does not threaten to destroy the world. He tells the workers exactly how much the next hour of water will cost.
bodyMovement: Othrek is fully human. A long mantle breaks his silhouette on one side; fitted ceramic and iron plates leave the hips and shoulders free to turn. The sluice-hook has a long reach and a real recovery when its weight commits.

The left gauntlet draws from a limited accumulator. Its valve releases a white plume before a short pressure burst, then needs a refill at a court standpipe. The player can interrupt the refill or cut off that supply. No unexplained infinite ammunition or invulnerable cutscene phase is required.
foodWeb: Role: a human consumer and controller of the institutions that distribute water and fish. His ecological power comes from infrastructure, labor and coercion, not a predatory species identity.
Dependency: keeper expertise, maintained gates, loyal guards and a working refill standpipe. Break those dependencies and his authority becomes physically vulnerable.
Disturbance: deliberate migration barriers and saline diversion produce linked damage in the Spawning Stair and Glassroot archive.
After victory: skilled workers and public oversight must operate the water system. Defeating the ruler opens a possibility; a transparent allocation schedule turns it into a durable gain.

encounter.objective: Defeat Othrek, stop the punitive saline release and reopen the civilian water line. The encounter combines a readable human duel with a limited environmental weapon.

phases.title: The price of passage
phases.description: A planted leading heel and a drawn-back hook announce a committed sweep. Stay outside its first arc, counter during the recovery and distinguish the gauntlet's white-plume cue from the blade cue. Solid pier cover blocks the pressure burst; an ordinary parry does not.

phases.title: Authority needs hands
phases.description: At half accumulator pressure Othrek calls two guards and moves toward a refill standpipe. One guard carries the gate key; the other protects the refill. Interrupt the supply, separate the guards with the court's existing cover and use a previously helped worker's signal to keep the drinking-water line open.

phases.title: The last levy
phases.description: With the accumulator disabled, Othrek fights a faster but shorter human duel and orders the saline bypass opened. His off-hand reaches toward the control chain before each command. One ally or a secured worker must hold the bypass shut while the duelist exploits his final overcommitted hook strike. Defeat ends the combat; control of the gate is the visible victory.

endings.label: Defeat and arrest the regent
endings.consequence: Workers secure Othrek after the duel and preserve his orders for a public hearing. The water line reopens immediately; the next chapter concerns testimony and a keeper council that can resist another monopoly.

endings.label: Kill Othrek and open the gate
endings.consequence: His command ends and the bypass closes. The victory is real; surviving officers may contest the record, so workers need the captured orders and a functioning public schedule rather than a replacement strongman.

endings.label: Force his guard to abandon him
endings.consequence: Expose the sabotage orders, disable the refill and protect the guards' families before the final exchange. The guard withdraws support and the defeated marshal yields; the council inherits trained operators instead of another mass grave.

entries.name: The Brine Tribunal
entries.title: Where the river is made to pay
entries.summary: A tidal fortress separates freshwater from salt and turns the crossing into a toll. Reach its exposed court, secure the bypass and win the river back.
history: The Tribunal's two sluice towers once kept storm tides out of a shared freshwater store. Its narrow court allowed keepers on both sides to inspect the same gate positions. Othrek converted that public checkpoint into a dueling ground and restricted access to the maintenance ledges.

Salt workers still live beside the pans, and the fortress still performs necessary flood work. The party cannot solve the region by collapsing every wall. Its best victory keeps the useful system intact while taking the coercive command away from the marshal.
storySeeds: Write a worker's account of the first day water is allocated publicly. Include one practical disagreement that survives liberation.
Let a character find a beautifully maintained mechanism and the cruel order it was used to execute. Make both facts matter.

image.alt: Two enormous rectangular sluice towers frame a narrow court; workers open a drinking-water tap above separate water channels, with a lower service ledge and an internal counterweight stair.

entries.artNote: The painting establishes the causeway, towers, workers and alternate route types. Channel colors alone cannot identify freshwater versus brine. Exact eighty-metre height, valve connectivity and continuous traversal require a playable layout.

growth.practice: Understand an arena before entering its central duel. Locate cover, the refill standpipe, the civilian line and a second route to the bypass.
growth.mastery: Reach the court with a worker ally, stop the punitive release and retain the operating records while defeating the garrison's command.
growth.reward: A public estuary crossing and keeper-operated cistern become a returnable community hub in the proposed campaign. Later visits can show reliable water, returning fish and an open market.
growth.rematch: A storm-defense challenge uses the same fortress after liberation. Players cooperate with former opponents to close tidal gates, proving that mastery includes protecting what they won.

sessionKit.prompt: Write or run a scene around The Brine Tribunal. Begin with a visible ecological clue, teach one safe response before escalating danger, and make victory change a named person's next day. Preserve the selected outcome and distinguish these EXPERIMENTAL proposals from locked Arcanea canon.
beats: Start at the locked tap, where the reason to fight is ordinary and immediate.
Offer the causeway, maintenance ledge and counterweight stair as distinct approaches.
Secure a worker who can close the bypass while the party confronts Othrek.
Return after victory to show a changed water queue and an open gate.

place.spatialIdentity: A narrow diagonal causeway reaches a court between two monumental rectangular sluice towers. Separate walled channels carry river water and tide; deep gate slots expose counterweights and maintenance stairs.
ecology: The estuary is a transition between freshwater and marine habitats. Its channels cannot be treated as interchangeable water effects.
Salt pans support livelihoods, while freshwater stores support drinking and seed nurseries. Allocation creates a political conflict with physical consequences.
Migration barriers at the stair and saline diversion at the archive are connected abuses of this operating system. The evidence trail makes the three new pairs one regional story.
After liberation, monitoring and seasonal gate schedules matter. A return visit should show whether the new council actually kept the promised passage open.
routes: Main causeway: visible, fast and exposed to Othrek's polearm reach; pier recesses provide real burst cover.
Water-level maintenance ledge: a quieter approach to the refill supply and bypass linkage, accessible only at a safe tide.
Counterweight stair: a vertical route to the operating records and signal balcony; moving weights create a timed traversal challenge with audible warning.
discoveries: Signed closure orders match the Spawning Stair's locked passage.
A bypass schedule matches the first salt-contaminated samples in the Glassroot archive.
A public operating manual proves the fortress can function without hereditary command, provided trained keepers and oversight survive.
place.consequence: The duel should end with an observable gain: taps run, the punitive bypass closes and workers cross the court freely. The proposed next chapter tests how the community keeps that gain through a storm.
